spectrum.interested: In a hypothetical relationship, tentative engagement might look like someone who asks what a group needs before proposing a specific step. They may explain a process and check whether you are the right person to act. You can test interest by seeing whether they name the decision-maker and the affected people, or whether they stay vague.
spectrum.invested: Observable follow-through would be filing the proposal, naming the body that must adopt it, and returning with the outcome. A real-life test is whether they accept that the group's vote belongs to the group. If they claim credit for a decision they only proposed, that is a limit to note.
spectrum.done: An actual boundary or exit appears when someone keeps asking you to act on a request that is not yours to decide, or when they treat your no as obstruction. A clear sign is repeated pressure after you have said the decision sits elsewhere. You can name that limit and step back without turning it into a debate about motives.

works.point: Identify who votes on the request
works.detail: Before asking for support, say who has the authority to adopt or reject the request. This prevents a discussion from turning into a general argument about values. In a meeting, you might say, 'The committee votes on Thursday, so our ask is for the three members who sit on it.'

When you draft a resolution or a proposal, state clearly that it is a proposal until the body acts. This keeps credit and responsibility where they belong. A practical sentence is, 'I filed this, but the group has not adopted it yet.'

If a bill or policy defines terms in ways that affect who can get care, show the link with a concrete example. Avoid abstract labels. You could ask, 'If this definition passes, which patients lose coverage?' and let the answer guide the request.

Formal proposals suit bodies with rules, while public explanation suits broader audiences. Match your channel to the decision you need. If you need a vote, prepare a short formal ask; if you need public awareness, prepare a plain explanation of the stakes.

In any advocacy, describe who faces the barrier and what specific change would help. This keeps the request from becoming about the advocate. For example, 'Women in rural clinics need this language clarified so they can get contraception without delay.'

never.point: Claiming the body's decision
never.detail: Do not say a group adopted something when you only proposed it. That confuses a member's action with the legislature's. If you catch yourself doing it, correct the record and name the vote.

never.point: Equating a definition with a motive
never.detail: Opposing a bill's language does not prove what its sponsors intended. Keep the critique on the observable effect. Say what the text would do to access, not what you believe is in someone's heart.

never.point: Using expertise as a wall
never.detail: Explaining a legal instrument can inform, but it can also shut down questions if it becomes a lecture. Invite one practical question before moving to the ask. This keeps the exchange two-way.

never.point: Turning affected people into props
never.detail: When you speak for people facing barriers, do not use their situation as a rhetorical device. Name the barrier and the requested change without dramatizing. If you are unsure, ask whether the people affected would recognize your description.

never.point: Pressuring the wrong person
never.detail: If someone says the decision is not theirs, do not keep pushing them as if they are the body. Identify the actual decision-maker or step away. Persistence aimed at the wrong target becomes pressure, not advocacy.

power_moves.name: Committee referral as a gate
power_moves.how_it_works: A person in a coordinating role can route a proposal to a subgroup, which then decides whether it advances. This is a legitimate procedural step, but it can also slow or bury a request. Observably, the chair frames the issue and the subgroup votes.
power_moves.defense: Ask for the referral date and the subgroup's decision timeline in writing. If the timeline keeps moving without a vote, say, 'I need a date when this will be decided or returned to the full group.'

power_moves.name: Definitional framing
power_moves.how_it_works: How a policy defines a term can change who qualifies for a benefit or protection. A communicator may argue that a bill's definition wrongly merges two categories, as Santiago did when she said contraception was being equated with abortion. This mechanism can clarify or obscure, depending on the text.
power_moves.defense: Request the exact clause and a concrete example of who would be affected. Then ask, 'Show me how this definition changes access for a person in this situation.'

power_moves.name: Public statement as pressure
power_moves.how_it_works: A statement outside formal proceedings can signal urgency and invite public attention. It may move a body to act, but it also risks hardening positions. The observable choice is whether the statement names a specific requested change or stays at the level of general concern.
power_moves.defense: Check whether the statement includes a clear ask and a named decision-maker. If you are the target, respond to the ask rather than the tone, and state what you can and cannot do.

power_moves.name: Sponsorship as explicit support
power_moves.how_it_works: Sponsoring a resolution puts a person's name on a proposal and signals they will shepherd it. This can lend credibility, but it also ties the sponsor to the outcome. The distinction is between support and control: the body still decides.
power_moves.defense: If you sponsor something, say plainly, 'I support this proposal, but the vote is not mine alone.' If you are asked to sponsor, ask what the sponsor is expected to do and what happens if the body rejects it.

power_moves.name: Access argument
power_moves.how_it_works: Framing a policy around who can actually obtain care shifts attention from labels to consequences. Santiago's statement argued that certain bills threatened women's access. This can make a technical dispute tangible, but it can also oversimplify if the evidence is thin.
power_moves.defense: Ask for one concrete case where access would change. Then separate the case from the broader claim. Say, 'I accept this example. Now show me whether the bill's text would produce it widely.'

leverage.point: Ask for the vote, not the vibe
leverage.detail: When you need a decision, request a specific action from the body that can take it. For example, 'Please put this on the agenda for the next meeting and record a vote.' This gives you a clear outcome to observe rather than a general expression of support.

A short written ask with the decision-maker, the requested action, and the date reduces confusion. You might send a one-paragraph note: 'I am asking the committee to endorse the proposal by Friday.' Written requests also help you distinguish a proposal from an adopted decision.

leverage.point: Separate the person from the decision
leverage.detail: If a senator or colleague says they support something, ask what they can actually do. Say, 'I hear your support. Will you vote for it, and can you confirm that in the minutes?' This keeps you from treating sympathy as a commitment.

leverage.point: Use a concrete example of harm
leverage.detail: When arguing about a definition, bring one real case of a person affected and ask how the text would change their access. For instance, 'This patient was refused contraception under the old rule. Would the new definition change that?' This grounds the discussion in observable effects.

leverage.point: Set a boundary on repeated asks
leverage.detail: If someone keeps pressing you to decide something that belongs to another body, name the limit. You could say, 'I cannot adopt this. The board votes on Tuesday, and I will pass your request to them.' Then step back and let the decision-maker respond.

closest.rationale: Like an advocate, she made specific requests to the body that could act—the Senate—on behalf of people facing barriers: victims of international crimes and women affected by restrictive bills. Her requests were concrete and directed at decision-makers.

cousin.tell: The Bridge Builder would bring the bill's sponsors and the women's health providers into one room to clarify terms before any resolution. Santiago instead filed a specific resolution for the Senate to concur with the Rome Statute and publicly opposed the domestic bills, directing her requests at the body that could act rather than convening the disputants. That difference is observable in her choice of channel and target, not a claim about her private temperament.

basis.style: Sponsors a resolution to extend a treaty's protection to future victims
basis.observation: Santiago used her committee chair to push for Philippine ratification of the Rome Statute, urging the Senate to concur and arguing that joining the court would help end impunity. She also publicly opposed domestic bills that she said restricted reproductive health care, framing the issue around women's access.

sections.identity: President of Indonesia who relied on statutory instruments for security policy.

matches.why: The source documents Megawati's use of a presidential decree to activate a pre-existing law, showing a procedural approach to a security question. The November extension is attributed to the government, not to her personally.

pattern: In October 2003, at a Bali press conference, Megawati itemized the subjects she and George Bush discussed, including counterterrorism, democratization support, military cooperation and post-IMF economic aid, and noted agreement on religious tolerance. The choice is a public list rather than a mood. Naming the agenda lets a reader distinguish a person who answers with enumerated topics from one who answers with atmosphere. A household analog is the family member who, asked about the weekend, names the driving, the budget and the in-law visit before any feeling surfaces. The list tells you where to probe and what got left off.

Her ratification of a treaty in Jakarta on 13 October 2003 was witnessed by State Secretary Bambang Kesowo and recorded in the State Gazette. A signature alone would be a gesture. Registration converts it into a checkable entry. The observable distinction is between an announcement and an act that leaves a paper trail someone else can find. In ordinary collaboration, that is the colleague who says 'let's put the change in the shared file' instead of 'let's agree to improve things.' Ask which register will hold your arrangement before treating it as settled.

In May 2003 she issued a decree making Law No. 23/1959 the legal basis for martial law in Aceh, and in November the government extended martial law while arguing it was needed to secure the 2004 elections. The decree activated an existing statute rather than drafting a fresh one. That is a procedural move, and it produced grave consequences for people living under the measures. Observably, she reached for the law book when a dispute about how to decide arose. A reader can learn to ask who bears the cost when procedure substitutes for deliberation. The extension belongs to the government's decision, not to her alone.

She was sworn in on 23 July 2001, moving from the vice presidency after Abdurrahman Wahid's impeachment proceedings in the People's Consultative Assembly. The sequence matters. The assembly decided impeachment. She assumed office through a transfer with a visible institutional author. That is different from claiming a mandate from nowhere. When you inherit a role midstream, the same question becomes practical: can you say who handed the task to you and what they decided? Naming the decider clarifies what is yours to change and what needs their return.

text: Her public manner in the documented moments is agenda-first and record-second. She lists topics with a counterpart, then her office files ratification with a witness and a gazette entry. Used across a disagreement, that sequence asks: what are we talking about, and where will the result live? It works best when the other person also gets to name items. A meeting that opens with a shared written agenda and closes with a shared written outcome tends to finish business.

There is a cost to treating the instrument as the conversation. The martial law decree and the government's later extension framed a severe security policy through legal steps while many people experienced its effects. A person can imitate the procedural clarity without noticing that the people most affected were not the ones naming the topics. Before borrowing her method, separate the question of how a decision is made from the question of who sits at the table. Where the second question goes unanswered, procedure can close a discussion rather than open it.
examples: At a Bali press conference in October 2003, Megawati listed counterterrorism, democratization support, military cooperation and post-IMF economic aid as topics she and George Bush discussed, noting agreement with him on religion tolerance.
Megawati ratified the treaty in Jakarta on 13 October 2003, with State Secretary Bambang Kesowo, and the ratification was recorded in the State Gazette of the Republic of Indonesia.

In May 2003 Megawati issued a presidential decree making Law No. 23/1959 the legal basis for martial law in Aceh. In November 2003 the Indonesian government extended the imposition of martial law, arguing it was needed to secure the 2004 elections.
Megawati was sworn in on 23 July 2001 to the presidency, stepping up from the vice presidency she had assumed after Abdurrahman Wahid's impeachment proceedings in the People's Consultative Assembly.

spectrum.interested: Tentative engagement looks like listing the items you want to settle and asking whether that list is complete. Tie each item to a place it will be recorded, such as a shared note or a calendar entry. Keep the list short and leave an opening for the other person to add or strike one item before anything is treated as agreed.
spectrum.invested: Invested follow-through is a completed record: a signed document, a witnessed step, a filed entry that another person can locate without your help. One test is whether a third party could reconstruct what you agreed from what you left behind. If the only evidence is your memory of the conversation, the decision is not yet anchored.
spectrum.done: A real boundary appears when procedure is used to prevent your item from being named, or when ratification happens without your access to the record. Say clearly that you need the decision held somewhere you can check and that you need your concern listed alongside the others. If both requests are refused, treat the gap as your answer rather than continuing to discuss it.

works.detail: Start a serious talk by naming the topics you believe belong on the table, as Megawati did with her counterpart in Bali. Invite additions explicitly. A list that only you can edit is an announcement, not a shared agenda.

works.point: Name the keeper of the record
works.detail: Decide who files the outcome and where, the way a ratification gets a witness and a gazette entry. Say aloud which document or thread you will both consult next month. This prevents later disputes about what was actually decided.

When a policy or plan will bind other people, ask separately how it was authorized and who will feel it. Write the two answers in different places. Mixing them lets formal correctness drown out lived impact.

works.point: State who handed you the task
works.detail: If you inherit work midstream, say which group or person assigned it and what they decided. This matches a transfer made by an assembly rather than a self-chosen mandate. Colleagues then know whom to approach for changes.

works.point: Let the other party reopen the list
works.detail: Close a procedural session by asking whether any item should be removed before it becomes fixed. Scheduling that question is a small act of consent. It keeps a documented decision from becoming a trap for someone who was not ready to agree.

never.point: Mistaking a decree for a debate
never.detail: Formal authorization can carry a decision past people it will hurt. Before invoking a rule to settle a live disagreement, ask whether anyone affected has had a chance to speak. If not, the procedural move is premature, however correct it looks.

never.point: Substituting registration for consent
never.detail: A filed entry proves a decision was recorded, not that everyone accepted it. Do not let a gazette-style record stand in for a yes from the person most directly concerned. Treat the record as evidence of process, not as proof of agreement.

never.point: Extending someone else's arrangement in their name
never.detail: The November extension belonged to the government's decision rather than to her personal action. In a team, if you renew an arrangement made by another person, say plainly whose arrangement it was and why it is continuing. Unattributed continuations breed resentment.

never.point: Choosing the statute before the aim
never.detail: Reaching for an existing law can feel decisive while leaving the actual purpose unexamined. Ask what outcome the rule is meant to serve and whether it fits. Choose the aim first, then the instrument that honors it.

never.point: Letting a witness become decoration
never.detail: A listed witness suggests oversight, but only if that person can object. Check that the role you assign has an exit or a veto. If the witness cannot say no, the appearance of accountability is empty.

power_moves.name: Agenda publication
power_moves.how_it_works: Announcing the topics of a meeting, as a press conference does, sets what counts as relevant before others arrive. Anyone who raises something off the list can be cast as disruptive. The mechanism is benign at its core and easy to weaponize by omission.
power_moves.defense: Ask to add one item before the agenda is frozen and note that request in the same place the agenda is kept. If the door does not open, the agenda is a fence rather than a plan.

power_moves.name: Instrumental ratification
power_moves.how_it_works: A signature with a witness and a registered entry turns an intention into a durable fact. People who expected further negotiation discover the matter is closed. The durability is a genuine service in many disputes and can foreclose discussion when it arrives early.
power_moves.defense: Ask when the record will be filed and whether any step remains open. If the answer is 'it's already done,' decide now whether you accept the terms or contest the filing.

power_moves.name: Pre-existing legal base
power_moves.how_it_works: Invoking an older law gives a decision the appearance of continuity with a settled order. The move can shield an actor from being seen as the origin of a hard policy. Observers should notice that continuity is being claimed, not that the rule perfectly fits the current problem.
power_moves.defense: Ask which rule was invoked, when it was written, and what changed since. Say which fit you question and propose the narrower application you could accept.

power_moves.name: Succession by procedure
power_moves.how_it_works: Stepping up after a formal assembly decision lends an officeholder an institutional pedigree. In a workplace, a person who inherits a role through a recorded selection can use that record to settle early doubt. It can also crowd out the question of whether the selection process was fair to everyone.
power_moves.defense: Name the body that decided and the questions it left unresolved. Ask for those questions to stay visible in the handover rather than being settled by the pedigree alone.

power_moves.name: Extension without the originator
power_moves.how_it_works: When a policy outlasts the moment that justified it, the person renewing it can attribute the continuation to circumstances or to a collective body. The originator's personal role fades from view. That can be honest delegation or a way to dilute responsibility.
power_moves.defense: Ask who is renewing what, and on whose authority. Write the answer down and check it against what the originator would have said.

leverage.detail: Tell the other person you would like the agreed item written where you can both reach it, and offer to do the writing yourself. It tests follow-through without making anyone confess to unreliability. Ask by when the entry will exist.

leverage.point: Keep your own copy of the list
leverage.detail: Before a meeting, write your four topics and bring a second copy for the other person. At the end, compare the two versions. Divergence tells you instantly whose framing carried the day.

When a procedure is about to bind you or people you care about, ask whether those affected have had a chance to respond. Require a concrete answer. An unwillingness to identify who was consulted is itself information.

Agree on a calendar date for the documented step, not just the intent. State that you will treat the arrangement as unsettled until the entry appears. Then hold that line rather than renegotiating the same promise.

Say in advance which outcome would end the cooperation, for example a decision taken without your listed item and without a route to reopen it. Ordinary candor about endings makes the process less coercive for everyone at the table.

closest.rationale: The source documents Megawati's use of a presidential decree to activate a pre-existing law, showing a procedural approach to a security question. The November extension is attributed to the government, not to her personally.

cousin.tell: The proceduralist, like Megawati issuing the May 2003 decree that made an existing law the basis for martial law in Aceh, agrees on the legal route and then leaves a record others can check. The co-builder would have wanted the people implementing and living under the policy to shape the route itself, which is a different demand and a fair test for a reader deciding whom to invite into a contentious plan.

basis.style: Legalistic and institutional
basis.observation: The public act most specific to the existing matched behaviour is Megawati's May 2003 presidential decree that made an existing statute the legal basis for martial law in Aceh. This decision was later extended by the Indonesian government in November 2003.

sections.identity: Indonesia's finance minister who steered pandemic spending toward health and small firms, then tied World Bank capital to a shareholding review.

matches.why: Like a person who asks the question that comes before the disputed one, she reframed a budget dispute as a prior question about who the institution serves and how it is governed, so the later spending choice follows from that.

pattern: In a World Bank Live discussion on financing an equitable recovery, she described Indonesia's pandemic budget as concentrating on health, social safety nets and small and medium enterprises while also deepening tax reform. The observable move is to name the current allocation and the structural change together, so the emergency response and the longer fiscal repair appear as one package rather than competing priorities. That lets a reader distinguish a reframer from someone who simply lists spending categories.

At the April 2024 Development Committee meeting, speaking for eleven countries, she welcomed the World Bank Group Evolution Roadmap and argued that a capital increase tied to a shareholding review would strengthen legitimacy and governance. Here the reframing is procedural. She treats the capital question as following from a prior decision about who the institution answers to, so the funding choice becomes a consequence of governance rather than a standalone ask. That distinction matters when someone tries to settle a budget without agreeing on decision rights.

When welcoming a development policy loan, she said that since 2019 the Indonesian government had focused on tax and expenditure reforms and that the support would strengthen fiscal sustainability and spur broad-based growth after the pandemic. The pattern is to connect an external endorsement to an internal reform track already underway, which keeps the emphasis on local choices rather than borrowed credit. A reader can use that distinction to separate a welcome that names prior work from one that simply celebrates the money.

As World Bank managing director and chief operating officer from 2010, she oversaw operations worldwide, shaped strategy for the Fund for the Poorest, IDA, and chaired the bank's Advisory Council on Gender and Development. That combination of operational scope and a dedicated advisory role shows a preference for pairing a broad mandate with a specific lens. The observable trait is not a claim about her private motives but a repeated public habit of attaching a particular question about who is served to a general institutional task.

text: Her contributions in multilateral settings tend to open with a welcome for the direction already on the table before she names a condition. At the Development Committee, she welcomed the Evolution Roadmap and then linked a capital increase to a shareholding review, which keeps the tone collaborative while making the sequencing explicit. That order gives listeners a clear point to respond to: first the governance question, then the funding decision. It is a practical way to disagree without starting from a veto.

In the World Bank Live discussion she spoke as a finance minister describing her own government's choices: health, social safety nets, small and medium enterprises, and deeper tax reform. The communication invites scrutiny of the allocation itself rather than a debate about intentions. For a reader in a workplace disagreement, the parallel is to state what your group is already doing and where the structural change must land, so others can test the plan against specifics instead of arguing about motives.

spectrum.interested: In a hypothetical collaboration, an interested counterpart might ask which prior question your proposal depends on and offer to settle that first. Tentative engagement looks like naming the governance or purpose issue before debating the budget line. You would see a request to clarify who decides, not a demand for immediate agreement.
spectrum.invested: An invested counterpart follows through by bringing the prior question to the table and proposing a sequence. Observable follow-through is a concrete step such as agreeing on decision rights before allocating resources. A real-life test is whether they return with a written sequencing proposal rather than a restated demand for the original outcome.
spectrum.done: A boundary appears when the other person keeps treating the prior question as a delaying tactic and insists on the spending decision without addressing governance. If repeated requests to settle the sequencing are met with avoidance, that is distinct from a difference of opinion. You can name the limit once and then decide whether to continue without the agreed frame.

works.point: Ask what must be settled first
works.detail: When a disagreement stalls on a number, ask what decision about purpose or decision rights must come first. State the question in one sentence and invite the other person to confirm or amend it before returning to the budget.

works.point: Pair current action with structural change
works.detail: Describe what your group is already doing and the reform that must accompany it. This mirrors the pandemic budget approach of naming health, safety nets and small enterprises alongside tax reform, so listeners see a package rather than a list.

works.point: Welcome the direction before the condition
works.detail: Open by acknowledging the proposal on the table, then state the sequencing condition. At the Development Committee she welcomed the roadmap before linking capital to a shareholding review. You can say you support the goal and then specify what must precede the funding decision.

works.point: Connect external support to internal work
works.detail: If an outside endorsement arrives, tie it to reforms your group has already undertaken. This keeps the emphasis on local choices and gives the other person a specific track record to examine rather than a general promise.

works.point: Use a specific lens on a broad mandate
works.detail: When a task feels too wide, attach a particular question about who is served. The advisory council on gender and development alongside worldwide operations shows how a focused lens can sit inside a large portfolio. You can propose one such lens and ask whether it changes the priorities.

never.point: Treat reframing as avoidance
never.detail: Redirecting to governance is not a way to dodge the budget question forever. If you raise the prior question, commit to returning to the original decision once it is settled. Otherwise the other person has grounds to see the move as stalling.

never.point: Confuse a constituency with a single voice
never.detail: Speaking for eleven countries means the statement reflects a collective position, not only a personal preference. In a meeting, do not present your own reframing as the group's view unless you have checked with the people you claim to represent.

never.point: Let the condition swallow the welcome
never.detail: A welcome that is immediately buried by conditions sounds like a veto. Keep the acknowledgment brief and genuine before naming the sequencing. The other person should be able to hear that the direction is accepted even if the order of decisions is disputed.

never.point: Assume the prior question settles everything
never.detail: Agreeing on governance does not automatically produce a fair allocation. The pandemic budget still had to name health, safety nets and small enterprises as priorities. After the prior question is resolved, return to the concrete choices and test them against the agreed frame.

never.point: Use institutional language as a shield
never.detail: Phrases like legitimacy and governance can obscure a simple disagreement about who decides. If you use them, add a plain statement of what you want to happen next. Otherwise the other person may hear abstraction where you intended a proposal.

power_moves.name: Sequencing shift
power_moves.how_it_works: The conversation moves from a disputed amount to a question about decision rights or purpose. This can be a genuine attempt to solve the underlying blockage or a way to delay a choice you dislike. The observable effect is that the original decision is postponed until the new question is addressed.
power_moves.defense: Ask the other person to state when the original decision will be revisited and what evidence would satisfy the prior question. Agree on a date and a criterion before accepting the reframe.

power_moves.name: Legitimacy linkage
power_moves.how_it_works: A funding or resource request is tied to a governance review, so support becomes conditional on institutional change. The mechanism can build trust by making the terms explicit, or it can raise the bar so high that the request never proceeds.
power_moves.defense: Separate the governance review into its own timeline and ask what specific change would unlock the funding. If the linkage keeps expanding, propose a parallel track with a fixed review point.

power_moves.name: Constituency cover
power_moves.how_it_works: A speaker presents a position as representing a group of countries or colleagues. This can lend weight and signal coordination, or it can make individual objections harder to voice. The observable move is to speak in the plural without naming who authorized the statement.
power_moves.defense: Ask which members of the constituency have endorsed the position and whether dissenting views will be recorded. If you are part of the group, request that your reservation be noted alongside the collective statement.

power_moves.name: Package presentation
power_moves.how_it_works: Emergency spending and structural reform are presented as one package, so rejecting one part appears to reject the whole. This can clarify trade-offs, or it can bundle a controversial change with an urgent need. The effect is to narrow the space for partial agreement.
power_moves.defense: Ask for the package to be unpacked into separate decisions with separate votes or review points. You can support the emergency component while reserving judgment on the structural reform.

power_moves.name: Broad mandate, specific lens
power_moves.how_it_works: A wide operational role is paired with a focused advisory council or lens. This can bring attention to an underserved question, or it can create an expectation that one lens should dominate all decisions. The observable pattern is a specific question attached to a general task.
power_moves.defense: Clarify whether the lens is advisory or decision-making and how its recommendations will be weighed against other priorities. Ask for the criteria in writing so the lens does not become an unspoken veto.

leverage.point: Request the governance question in writing
leverage.detail: When a discussion loops on a number, request that the other person write down the governance or purpose question they believe must come first. Say you will respond to that question in writing before returning to the budget. This gives you a concrete artifact to test and prevents the reframe from remaining vague.

If you accept a sequencing shift, propose a specific date to revisit the original decision and a criterion for what counts as settled. Say you are willing to discuss the prior question until that date and then expect to return to the allocation. This keeps the reframe from becoming an indefinite delay.

When emergency spending and structural reform are bundled, ask for two separate decisions. State that you can support the urgent component now and will review the structural change on its own timeline. This lets you act on the immediate need without endorsing a reform you have not examined.

If someone speaks for a group, ask which members have agreed and whether your view will be recorded. Say you want to support the collective statement but need your reservation noted. This tests whether the plural voice is authorized and protects your position within the group.

leverage.point: Name the lens and its limits
leverage.detail: When a broad task is paired with a specific lens, ask how that lens will be weighed against other priorities. Propose that its recommendations be advisory for a fixed period and then reviewed. This keeps a useful focus from quietly becoming the only criterion.

closest.rationale: Like a person who asks the question that comes before the disputed one, she reframed a budget dispute as a prior question about who the institution serves and how it is governed, so the later spending choice follows from that.

cousin.tell: The Translator would take the same Development Committee moment and first restate the capital increase in plain terms, then ask the listener what they heard before moving to governance. Sri Mulyani Indrawati instead makes the governance question the entry point and treats the capital decision as following from it. The cousin checks comprehension, while this pattern checks the sequence of decisions, and you can tell which is happening by whether the next move is a paraphrase or a procedural proposal.

basis.style: recasts fiscal strain as an SDG financing question before the committee
basis.observation: In her 2024 Development Committee statement she moved the debate from short-term pandemic losses to the long-run SDG financing gap and the bank's own capital and governance structure. She framed a capital increase as the prior question of institutional legitimacy that must be settled before funding decisions can follow.

sections.identity: Thailand's prime minister in 2011, she briefed a visiting UN secretary-general on both flood relief and a national reconciliation dialogue in the same appearance.

matches.why: A reframer asks the question that comes before the stuck decision. Here the immediate decision was flood response, and her briefing moved the frame to include a reconciliation dialogue as the longer-term question, though the source records her briefing rather than a deliberate reframing of a specific decision.

pattern: When flooding struck Thailand in 2011, Yingluck Shinawatra briefed UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon in Bangkok on the emergency response and on efforts toward a national reconciliation dialogue. She treated the political track as a parallel question to immediate relief, not as a separate issue. This shows a habit of widening the frame when facing a crisis. In your own stuck decision, consider asking what longer-term question sits alongside the urgent one.

After a coalition of four smaller parties formed following the 2011 election, the governing arrangement earned an Inter-Parliamentary Union note on reconciliation and political-party dissolution. Yingluck Shinawatra's leadership involved managing a multiparty coalition, which required balancing diverse interests. For a reader, this points to the value of recognizing when a solution needs to accommodate several stakeholders, not just the loudest voice.

In Seoul in 2012, Yingluck Shinawatra updated Ban Ki-moon on flood recovery and heard his emphasis on genuine national reconciliation for long-term stability. She exchanged views on regional and development issues. This kind of exchange suggests a willingness to bring external perspectives into internal debates. If you are stuck, you might invite an outsider to reflect back what they hear, which can reveal assumptions you missed.

In December 2012, Yingluck Shinawatra and Myanmar's President visited the Dawei Special Economic Zone, a cross-border industrial project. This joint visit underscores a focus on regional cooperation and long-term economic development. It illustrates how reframing can involve looking beyond immediate borders to shared futures. In personal negotiations, you might ask what a broader, mutually beneficial outcome could look like.

text: Yingluck Shinawatra's briefing to Ban Ki-moon in Bangkok linked flood response with reconciliation talks. She presented these as connected tracks, not separate items. This communication choice suggests an ability to hold multiple threads in one conversation. When you speak, you might explicitly name how an immediate task connects to a longer-term goal, helping others see the bigger picture.

In Seoul, she updated Ban on flood recovery and received his emphasis on reconciliation. The exchange was two-way, with views shared on regional and development issues. This back-and-forth indicates a communication style that invites input. In your own discussions, you could ask for the other person's perspective on long-term stability, showing that you value their insight as part of the solution.

spectrum.interested: In a hypothetical relationship analogy, a tentative version of this pattern might look like someone who, when a practical problem arises, mentions a related long-term concern without pushing it. They test whether you see the connection. You might respond by acknowledging the link and asking which aspect feels most pressing to them.
spectrum.invested: An invested version would show follow-through by regularly bringing both immediate and long-term matters into conversations. One real-life test: do they check back on how you felt about the wider frame they introduced? If they adjust based on your feedback, that signals genuine investment in shared understanding.
spectrum.done: A boundary becomes clear when someone repeatedly reframes without checking your readiness, or dismisses your need to focus on the immediate. If you say, 'I need to solve this step first,' and they keep redirecting, that is a sign to set a firmer limit or step back.

works.detail: When stuck, explicitly say, 'Let's handle the urgent piece and also note the longer-term question.' This mirrors the practice of briefing on both flood response and reconciliation. It helps others see you are not ignoring either.
Ask a trusted person to reflect what they hear. Like the exchange in Seoul, an outsider can highlight the reconciliation angle you might miss. Frame it as seeking clarity, not judgment.

In group decisions, ask each stakeholder what they need. The coalition arrangement after 2011 required accommodating smaller parties. Similarly, ensure quieter voices are heard before finalizing plans.
Consider how a personal decision fits into a broader context, as with the Dawei cross-border project. Ask, 'What wider impact could this have?' This can reveal shared interests.

When reporting progress, invite the other person's emphasis. In Seoul, Yingluck received Ban's focus on reconciliation. Say, 'Here's where I am, and what do you see as key for stability?' This keeps communication reciprocal.

never.point: Assume buy-in
never.detail: Presenting a linked frame without checking how it lands can leave others feeling unheard. After you mention a longer-term concern, ask, 'Does that fit with your priorities?' to avoid imposing your view.

never.point: Overload the urgent
never.detail: Linking a crisis to a big political question might overwhelm someone focused on immediate needs. If the other person seems stressed, acknowledge the urgent first and defer the wider frame.

never.point: Ignore power gaps
never.detail: In coalition settings, smaller parties may have less leverage. If you are in a stronger position, explicitly invite dissent and protect quieter voices from being steamrolled.

never.point: Forget follow-up
never.detail: Introducing a long-term track without later revisiting it erodes trust. Schedule a check-in to see how the broader question is progressing, showing you take it seriously.

never.point: Use jargon
never.detail: Terms like 'reconciliation' can be abstract. Translate into concrete language: 'How do we repair trust?' or 'What would make you feel secure?' This keeps the conversation accessible.

power_moves.name: the parallel frame
power_moves.how_it_works: You introduce a related long-term question alongside an immediate task, hoping to expand the conversation. This can feel like a shift in focus. The other person may wonder if you are avoiding the urgent issue.
power_moves.defense: If someone does this to you, say, 'I see the connection, but let's finish the immediate step first.' This acknowledges their point while keeping boundaries.

power_moves.name: coalition building
power_moves.how_it_works: You bring in multiple parties to create a broader base, as with the four smaller parties. This can make decisions more inclusive but also more complex. Others might feel their individual concerns are diluted.
power_moves.defense: Ask, 'How will each voice be heard in this group?' Ensure there is a clear process for input and that smaller parties are not just rubber stamps.

power_moves.name: external validation
power_moves.how_it_works: You seek an outside authority's view, like the UN Secretary-General's emphasis, to lend weight to a direction. This can strengthen your position but may make the other person feel sidelined.
power_moves.defense: If you feel sidelined, say, 'I value outside input, but I need to hear your perspective directly too.' Request that the external view is balanced with your own.

power_moves.name: cross-border linking
power_moves.how_it_works: You connect a local issue to a larger regional or global project, as with Dawei. This can inspire but also seem distant from daily concerns. The other person might feel their immediate problem is being overshadowed.
power_moves.defense: Bring it back to the personal: 'How does this big picture affect what we need today?' Ask for concrete links to your shared reality.

power_moves.name: two-way briefing
power_moves.how_it_works: You share an update and invite the other's emphasis, creating a reciprocal exchange. This can build trust but may also be used to steer the conversation toward your preferred focus.
power_moves.defense: Notice if your emphasis is genuinely incorporated. If not, say, 'I shared my view, and I'd like to see it reflected in next steps.'

leverage.detail: When a discussion stalls, say, 'What question are we not asking?' This invites the reframer in you or the other person to surface the parallel track. It can unlock new options without dismissing the current one.

List everyone affected by a decision, including quieter parties. Ask each what they need. This mirrors coalition management and ensures no one is overlooked, making the eventual agreement more durable.

After introducing a longer-term concern, agree on a date to revisit it. Say, 'Let's check back in two weeks on how the big picture is affecting us.' This prevents the wider frame from being forgotten.
If someone uses a broad term like 'reconciliation,' ask, 'What would that look like in practice for you?' This grounds the conversation in concrete behaviors and expectations, making it actionable.

When you feel overwhelmed by immediate tasks, say, 'I need to focus on this now, but I also want to schedule time for the bigger question.' This honors both needs and sets a boundary against being pulled away prematurely.

closest.rationale: A reframer asks the question that comes before the stuck decision. Here the immediate decision was flood response, and her briefing moved the frame to include a reconciliation dialogue as the longer-term question, though the source records her briefing rather than a deliberate reframing of a specific decision.

cousin.tell: The Reframer, like Yingluck Shinawatra linking flood response to reconciliation, asks what question comes before the stuck decision. The Translator, by contrast, would first restate the flood response in simpler terms and then check if you heard the reconciliation point, ensuring mutual understanding before moving on. The difference lies in initiation versus verification: the Reframer introduces the parallel track, while the Translator confirms it was received.

sections.identity: Aung San Suu Kyi, the Burmese opposition figure who in 1988 proposed an independent committee to oversee a transition to multiparty elections.

matches.why: This is a proceduralist act because she named an independent body and elections as the rule for settling a disputed transition, making the outcome open to public verification.

pattern: In 1988 she wrote an open letter asking Burma’s government to bring independent figures into a committee overseeing a move to multiparty elections and to release political prisoners. The proposal located the authority in a checkable body rather than in herself. Readers can separate a demand for a fair procedure from a demand for personal loyalty. When someone suggests an independent panel for a disputed decision, ask who appoints it and what it publishes.

She helped found the National League for Democracy in September 1988 and, despite a ban on meetings, took its case to public gatherings around the country. The observable choice is persistence in the face of procedural obstruction. It lets a reader distinguish between a person who works around constraints and one who waits for perfect conditions. In everyday collaboration, notice whether a blocked plan leads to a smaller, lawful test or to silence.

On 16 June 2012 she delivered the Nobel lecture in Oslo City Hall, more than two decades after the 1991 award. The long gap between recognition and the act of speaking is a visible fact. It allows a reader to distinguish between symbolic honor and the effort of showing up in person. A useful parallel is a delayed acknowledgment: notice who finally appears and what they do with the platform.

On 11 December 2019 she appeared before the International Court of Justice to defend Myanmar in The Gambia’s case alleging genocide against the Rohingya. She spoke for the state whose conduct was at issue. The distinction is between representing an institution and endorsing every action taken in its name. A reader can ask who a speaker is authorized to represent and whether that role limits what they can say.

text: Her public communication often takes the form of a procedural proposal: an independent committee, an election, a court appearance. The 1988 open letter and the NLD’s public meetings show a preference for a stated mechanism over a private assurance. When someone in a group proposes a rule for deciding a disputed point, ask for the rule in writing and for a date when the result will be shown. That is a way to test whether the proposal is a genuine process or a delay.

She has also communicated through the act of showing up after long delays, as with the Nobel lecture, and through defending an institution in a legal forum, as at the ICJ. Those moves can be read as signals of commitment to a role rather than as statements of personal warmth. In your own conversations, watch whether a person’s commitment is expressed by attending a hard meeting or by defending an institution’s record. Ask what role they are speaking from before you treat their words as a personal promise.
examples: In an open letter in 1988, Aung San Suu Kyi urged Burma’s government to bring independent figures into a committee that could oversee a transition to multiparty elections. She also pressed for the release of political prisoners.
In September 1988 Aung San Suu Kyi helped establish the National League for Democracy. Despite a ban on meetings, she took its political case to public gatherings around the country.
On 16 June 2012 she travelled to Oslo City Hall to deliver the Nobel lecture associated with her 1991 Peace Prize. More than two decades separated the award from her appearance there in person.

On 11 December 2019 Aung San Suu Kyi appeared before the International Court of Justice to defend Myanmar in The Gambia’s case alleging genocide against the Rohingya. She spoke for the state whose conduct was at issue.

spectrum.interested: A person using this pattern might propose a small checkable step, such as a written summary or a named third party to review a decision. Tentative engagement looks like asking whether that step is acceptable. You can reply by naming one concrete condition you need, like a shared document or a date, before you agree to go further.
spectrum.invested: Observable follow-through includes showing up after a delay and defending a process even when it is unpopular. A real-life test is whether the person submits to the same independent check they propose for others. Ask them to put their own decision through the review they suggested. If they resist, that is information about the limits of their procedural commitment.
spectrum.done: A boundary is reached when the process is repeatedly postponed or when independent figures are excluded from a committee they were meant to join. If you have asked twice for a checkable step and received only assurances, treat that as an exit signal. Say plainly that you will not continue without the written rule, and then stop attending the meetings.

works.detail: When a group faces a disputed decision, propose a specific independent reviewer and a publication date. Ask for those two details in writing. This turns a vague promise into a testable commitment.

Before reacting to a strong statement, ask whether the person is speaking for themselves, a team or an institution. Their answer changes what you can reasonably expect them to concede. It also tells you whom to approach with a counter-proposal.

A long gap between an award and a speech shows that delay is not always abandonment. Ask what kept the process from happening and what would make it happen now. Set a review date rather than treating the delay as a final answer.

works.point: Use public meetings as a test
works.detail: When a decision is contested, observe whether the person takes the case to a wider group despite obstacles. If they do, ask what record of that meeting will be shared. That record is more useful than a private assurance.

works.point: Request a written rule for disagreement
works.detail: Propose that the next disputed point be settled by a rule agreed in advance, such as a vote or an outside review. Write the rule down and name the person who will confirm the outcome. This keeps the focus on the process rather than on personalities.

never.point: Treating a role as a personal promise
never.detail: A state representative defending a case is not making a private vow to you. Do not convert an institutional statement into a promise of personal loyalty. Ask what the person can decide as an individual before you rely on their words.

never.point: Ignoring the cost of persistence
never.detail: Taking a case to public gatherings under a ban carries risks that are not a template for ordinary conflict. Do not praise endurance without asking who bears the cost. In a team, check whether the same burden is being placed on the least powerful person.

never.point: Mistaking a committee for a solution
never.detail: An independent committee can be a genuine step or a way to postpone a decision. Do not accept the committee’s existence as proof that the dispute is settled. Ask for its members, its mandate and its first public report.

never.point: Assuming a delayed appearance erases the gap
never.detail: A speech given decades after an award does not undo the years of absence. Do not treat a late acknowledgment as full repair. Name what was missed and ask what specific action will follow the appearance.

never.point: Confusing defense of a state with defense of a person
never.detail: Speaking for a state at a court is not the same as speaking for every person affected by its conduct. Do not let a representative’s brief become a verdict on individual experiences. Keep the distinction between the institution’s case and the accounts of those harmed.

power_moves.name: The referral to an independent body
power_moves.how_it_works: A person facing a disputed decision proposes that an independent group review it, which can look like a fair process. The move can also stall a decision while appearing to honor procedure. The observable question is whether the group has named members and a deadline.
power_moves.defense: Ask for the group’s membership and its first reporting date in writing. If those cannot be given, treat the referral as a delay rather than a resolution.

power_moves.name: The long-arc appearance
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone returns to a commitment after a long gap, and the return itself becomes the story. This can signal endurance or it can distract from what happened during the absence. The distinction lies in what the person does after the appearance.
power_moves.defense: Acknowledge the appearance and then ask for one concrete action that follows it. Compare that action with what was promised before the gap.

power_moves.name: Speaking for the institution
power_moves.how_it_works: A person answers a challenge by adopting the voice of the organization they represent. This can make a personal disagreement sound like an institutional necessity. The move can limit what the person is able to concede without a mandate.
power_moves.defense: Ask whether the person is speaking with authority or only as a member. Request a separate conversation with the person who can actually decide.

power_moves.name: The public gathering despite a ban
power_moves.how_it_works: A meeting is held in defiance of a restriction, and the act of gathering becomes the message. This can demonstrate commitment, but it can also expose participants to consequences they did not choose. The visible choice is who is asked to take the risk.
power_moves.defense: Before joining, ask who has agreed to bear the cost of the gathering. If the risk falls on people who were not part of the decision, propose a smaller lawful step instead.

power_moves.name: The written proposal as a shield
power_moves.how_it_works: A detailed written proposal can be used to show good faith while leaving the actual decision untouched. The text becomes a substitute for a checkable outcome. The question is whether the proposal names a date and a person who will confirm the result.
power_moves.defense: Accept the written proposal only if it includes a deadline and a named reviewer. Set a follow-up meeting to check the result, and treat silence as a negative answer.

leverage.point: Demand a checkable step before agreeing
leverage.detail: When someone proposes a committee or a process, say that you will agree once the members and the first report date are named. This gives you a concrete reason to wait rather than argue about intentions. It also creates a record you can revisit.

leverage.point: Ask what role the speaker holds
leverage.detail: Before you accept a strong statement, ask whether the person is speaking for themselves or for a group. Their answer tells you whether a concession is within their power. If it is not, ask to be directed to someone who can decide.

leverage.point: Set a review date for a delayed commitment
leverage.detail: If a promised action has been delayed, propose a specific date to review it and write down what will count as done. This turns an open-ended delay into a test you can observe. It also prevents the delay from becoming the new normal without your consent.

When a group plans to push through an obstacle, ask who will bear the risk and whether they have agreed to it. Say that you will support a smaller lawful step if the burden is shared. This keeps a commitment from being built on someone else’s exposure.

leverage.point: Keep the institution and the person separate
leverage.detail: If a representative defends an institution’s record, ask what they can decide as an individual and what is outside their mandate. Use that distinction to decide whether to continue the conversation with them or with the institution. It prevents a role from being mistaken for a personal promise.

closest.rationale: This is a proceduralist act because she named an independent body and elections as the rule for settling a disputed transition, making the outcome open to public verification.

cousin.tell: The Proceduralist, as seen in Aung San Suu Kyi’s 1988 open letter, proposes an independent committee and elections as the rule for settling a transition. The Co-Builder would sit inside that committee, sharing the drafting and the public accounting of its decisions. The difference shows in who writes the rule and who merely asks for it to exist.

basis.style: urged an independent oversight committee and multiparty elections
basis.observation: In an open letter in 1988, Aung San Suu Kyi called on Burma's government to include independent figures in a committee to oversee a transition to multiparty elections and to release political prisoners. The proposal centered on a checkable mechanism rather than on her own authority.

sections.identity: Taiwan's president who stood at the Presidential Office entrance to apologize to indigenous peoples and convened a committee to carry the process forward.

matches.why: She set a rule and venue for how a contested question would be handled, making the procedure open to scrutiny by participants and the press.

pattern: In her first inaugural address she promised a national judicial congress for that October, naming a month before naming an outcome. The commitment was to a venue and a date, which anyone could check later. That lets a reader distinguish a person who wants a decision to be legitimate from one who merely wants the decision they prefer. When you propose a family or workplace decision, ask whether you have set a time and a place where everyone can see the choice being made.

At the 2016 indigenous apology ceremony, she spoke for the government and announced a committee she would personally convene. The procedural move came with a personal chair, not a delegate. That distinction matters because it shows where the responsibility for follow-through sits. In a shared project, when someone says 'we should look into that,' you can ask who will sit in the chair and when it first meets. If the answer is vague, the process is decorative.

The San Salvador bilateral talks in January 2017 paired closed-door discussion of trade and investment with a public honour afterward. Two registers, one visit. A reader can see how a formal meeting between officeholders can have a private working half and a visible ceremonial half without either cancelling the other. If you are negotiating something with a counterpart, decide in advance which parts are for the table and which are for the record, and tell the other person which is which.

At Columbia in 2019 she cited Taiwan's same-sex marriage law as evidence that progressive values could take root in an East Asian society. She did not describe the law as her personal gift but as a societal result. That is a small but real distinction between claiming an outcome and pointing to a change that many people made. When a team you lead achieves something, notice whether you describe it as a shared result or as your own. The first invites continued participation. The second ends it.

text: Her public language tends to sequence things. First the apology, then the committee, then the chair. First the congress, then the reform. The order is a form of respect for the people who will be affected because it tells them when their turn to speak arrives. In ordinary conversation, you can borrow the sequencing without the ceremony. Say what you are acknowledging, say what happens next, and say when. A partner who hears all three knows whether to stay engaged or to brace for another round of vague sympathy.

She also separates the bilateral from the ceremonial. The San Salvador talks produced a working conversation and a decoration, and she did not collapse them into one message. That separation is useful when you are handling a disagreement with someone you also need to thank. Keep the working conversation about the thing that is stuck. Keep the appreciation for the thing that is not. Mixing them makes both feel like leverage. Naming them apart makes both more credible.
examples: At a August 1, 2016 ceremony in the Presidential Office Building, Tsai apologized on behalf of the government to indigenous peoples and announced a Presidential Office committee on indigenous historical justice that she would personally convene.

In her May 20, 2016 inaugural address, Tsai pledged to hold a national congress on judicial issues that October, framing judicial reform as a process open to public participation rather than a predetermined verdict.

During an April 2019 Columbia University speech, Tsai recounted Taiwan's democratic transition and cited its recent same-sex marriage law as evidence that progressive values could take root in East Asian society.

At the Presidential House in San Salvador on January 13, 2017, Tsai held bilateral talks with President Salvador Sanchez Ceren on cooperation, trade and investment, then received the National Order of Jose Matias Delgado.

spectrum.interested: In a hypothetical relationship analogy, tentative engagement looks like proposing a specific conversation at a specific time about a topic neither of you has settled. You are not promising the outcome. You are promising the venue. That is the lowest-cost way to show you take the other person's stake seriously without pretending you already agree.
spectrum.invested: Observable follow-through is that the named conversation happens when it was said to happen, and that the other person can see who is responsible for the next step. A real-life test is whether you can point to a date and a chair. If the meeting slipped and no one said why, that is information. If it slipped and someone named the new date, that is also information.
spectrum.done: An actual boundary shows up when the process is used as a substitute for a decision that never arrives. If every request for a concrete answer produces another committee, another congress, another round of consultation, you are allowed to say the process has stopped being a commitment. The exit is a sentence, not a scene. Name the question, name the deadline, and say what you will do if neither is met.

works.point: Name the venue and the month
works.detail: When a group you are part of is stuck, propose a specific meeting time and a named person who will run it. Write both down where everyone can see them. The specificity is the courtesy.

works.point: Put the chair in the room
works.detail: If you are asking for a process, say who will be accountable for it by name. A committee without a chair is a wish. A chair without a date is a delay. Ask for both before you agree to wait.

works.point: Separate the working half from the ceremonial half
works.detail: When you have to both negotiate and thank someone, tell them which part of the conversation is which. 'I want to settle the schedule, and separately I want to say I am glad you came' is a sentence that keeps both halves honest.
If something went well in a group you are part of, describe it as something many people made. Use names. The habit costs little and keeps the people who did the work willing to do more.

works.point: Check the follow-through against the announcement
works.detail: After a public commitment, look for the date and the chair. If they are missing, ask for them in plain language. You are not being hostile. You are taking the announcement at its word.

never.point: Do not mistake an apology for a repair
never.detail: An apology that names a committee is a beginning, not an ending. If you are the one apologising, do not let the announcement stand in for the change. If you are the one receiving it, ask what happens after the committee reports.

never.point: Do not let procedure hide a decision you have already made
never.detail: A process that is open in name but closed in fact teaches people to disengage. If you have already decided, say so and let the conversation be about consequences. If you have not, mean it when you say the outcome is open.

never.point: Do not blur the two registers under pressure
never.detail: When a working conversation gets tense, do not reach for the ceremonial gratitude to soften it. That makes the thanks feel like a bargaining chip. Keep the two apart even when the room is small.

never.point: Do not claim a social change as a personal gift
never.detail: If many people worked for something, saying 'I did this' takes the result away from them. Say what the group did. Say what you did within it. The distinction is not modesty. It is accuracy.

never.point: Do not let the process become the point
never.detail: A committee that meets forever is a way of not deciding. If you are in charge of one, give it a reporting date and a question it must answer. If you are waiting on one, ask for the same.

power_moves.name: The named forum
power_moves.how_it_works: A disputed question is routed to a specific venue with a specific date, which makes the handling of the question visible even before the outcome is. The person proposing it gains credibility for openness and also sets the terms of the conversation.
power_moves.defense: Accept the forum and then ask who is in the room and what the reporting line is. If those answers are clear, the forum is real. If they are not, propose your own venue with your own date.

power_moves.name: The personal chair
power_moves.how_it_works: By convening the committee herself rather than delegating, the convener ties her own attention to the process. That raises the cost of letting it stall and signals to participants that the issue is not being parked.
power_moves.defense: Ask what the chair will do if the committee cannot agree. A chair who has an answer is invested. A chair who has only a title is decorating.

power_moves.name: The two-register visit
power_moves.how_it_works: A working meeting and a public honour happen on the same trip but are kept distinct. The counterpart can read the seriousness of the working half without having to interpret the ceremonial half as a concession.
power_moves.defense: When you are the counterpart, say which half you are in before you respond. 'I hear the thanks, and I want to go back to the trade question' keeps the registers from collapsing.

power_moves.name: The societal result
power_moves.how_it_works: A change is described as something a society achieved rather than something a leader granted. That framing invites continued participation and makes the change harder to reverse by attacking one person.
power_moves.defense: If you are credited with a group's result, add the names of the people who did the work. If you are the one doing the crediting, ask whether the leader is pointing to the group or to themselves.

power_moves.name: The sequenced acknowledgement
power_moves.how_it_works: An apology comes first, then the process, then the chair. The order tells affected people when their turn arrives and reduces the chance that the acknowledgement is heard as a substitute for action.
power_moves.defense: After an acknowledgement, wait for the date and the chair. If they arrive, the sequence is working. If only the acknowledgement arrives, say what you are still waiting for.

leverage.point: Ask for the date and the chair in one sentence
leverage.detail: When someone proposes a process, say: 'I am glad we are doing this. When does it first meet, and who is running it?' That sentence is not hostile. It takes the proposal seriously enough to want it to exist.

leverage.point: Say which half of the conversation you are in
leverage.detail: If you need to both appreciate someone and disagree with them, open by naming the half. 'I want to thank you for the help, and I also want to settle the schedule.' The other person can then respond to the right thing.

leverage.point: Put a reporting date on any committee you join
leverage.detail: Before you agree to serve, ask what question the group must answer and by when. If the answer is vague, propose a date yourself. A group that cannot name a reporting date is a way of waiting, not a way of deciding.

leverage.point: Name the shared result out loud
leverage.detail: When a group you are part of finishes something, say who did what. Use names. The habit is small and it keeps the people who did the unglamorous parts willing to do them again. It also makes your own credit more credible.

leverage.point: Treat a stalled process as a boundary question
leverage.detail: If the named date passes with no meeting and no new date, say so once, plainly. 'The meeting was set for October and it did not happen. What is the new date?' If there is no new date, you have learned what the process was for.

closest.rationale: She set a rule and venue for how a contested question would be handled, making the procedure open to scrutiny by participants and the press.

cousin.tell: Tsai Ing-wen's procedural style and the Co-Builder archetype both care about how a disputed decision is made, but they part company on who holds the pen. The named judicial congress was a forum she set and would open, while a Co-Builder would more likely insist that the agenda and the chair be shared from the start. The same gap appears in the indigenous committee: Tsai convened it personally, whereas a Co-Builder would ask the affected communities to co-write the terms before the first meeting. Neither is a claim about private warmth. It is a difference in where the authority sits when the process begins.

basis.style: Pledged an October national judicial congress so the reform process, not a verdict, would be public
basis.observation: In the 2016 inaugural address Tsai named a specific forum and month for judicial reform rather than announcing an outcome. The pledge made the deliberative step itself the visible commitment.

sections.identity: Taiwan's vice president from 2000 to 2008 who, speaking to Taiwanese-American students at Harvard in 2002, proposed that China and Taiwan each adopt freedom and democracy as a first system.

matches.why: Like a reframer who asks the question a different way when a conversation is stuck, Lu took an established policy phrase and substituted a prior question about sequencing systems, without demanding a bargain or making a reciprocal offer.

pattern: When Lu faced the cross-strait formula debate at a 2002 Harvard conference, she did not counter the sovereignty wording directly. She proposed that both sides first adopt freedom and democracy as their shared system. The observed move is to replace the contested question with a prior condition. Read that as a style of redirecting stuck talks: notice when someone swaps an end-state argument for a sequencing question, and ask whether the new question actually helps both sides move or merely changes the subject.

Her February 2006 tea party for female officials and elected representatives paired a concrete proposal with an existing project. She floated a nationwide association of women in political life to work alongside her Democratic Pacific Union. That connects a new network to something already running rather than starting from zero. In everyday terms, this is the colleague who suggests a joint effort and names which standing group it would attach to, which makes follow-through easier to imagine and to test.

In August 2005, after the Thai workers' riot in Kaohsiung, Lu visited the city and held the transit and labour management companies responsible while calling for a swift, thorough investigation. The observable choice is to name the parties she considers accountable and press for a process rather than to speak for the workers themselves. Readers can separate a demand for inquiry from the experience of the people harmed, which are not the same thing and should not be merged.

At the January 2004 ceremony for families of Kaohsiung Incident victims, Lu announced a "save Taiwan with peace" campaign, citing missile deployment and a right to a referendum. She tied commemoration to a forward-looking public appeal. A listener can notice how she converts a solemn occasion into a platform and then judge, independently, whether that suits the moment. The families' grief remains theirs and is not evidence about her private feelings.

text: Across these episodes, Lu tends to speak in proposals. She suggests a shared system, an association, an investigation, a campaign. Each is offered as a direction rather than a settled bargain, and she seldom presents reciprocal offers. When you hear language like this, sorting proposals from decisions helps. A proposal invites discussion and can be declined without insult. A decision by a legislature or agency binds people, and that act belongs to the body as a whole, not to one member who spoke about it.

Her public register is declarative and forward-leaning, often launching a phrase that reframes the topic. That can energise a room and also leave details thin. In working relationships, mirror the useful part by restating what you heard as a proposal and then asking what would make it concrete. Say plainly which parts you can support and which need more information before you commit. This keeps a good idea from being mistaken for a finished plan.
examples: On 24 August 2005 Vice President Lu visited Kaohsiung over the Thai workers' riot, holding the Kaohsiung Rapid Transit and Hua Pan labour management companies responsible and calling for a swift, thorough investigation.

On 14 February 2006 Vice President Lu convened female officials and elected representatives at a tea party, proposing a nationwide association for female political figures to work with her Democratic Pacific Union.
Speaking at the Harvard ITASA conference in 2002, Vice President Lu suggested that China and Taiwan each first adopt one system, namely freedom and democracy, instead of 'one country, two systems.'

At a January 2004 Taipei inauguration for victims' families of the Kaohsiung Incident, Vice President Lu announced a 'save Taiwan with peace' campaign citing China's missile deployment and Taiwan's right to a referendum.
